sections.normalized_html:
An ordinary differential equation with dependent variable [MATH: y] and independent variable [MATH: x] is said to be autonomous if it can be written in the form [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}=f(y),] or equivalently, [MATH: y'=f(y).]

With that in mind, let's check each of the differential equations:

  • Equation I is an autonomous differential equation. We see that it is of the form [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}=f(y),] where [MATH: f(y)= y^3.]

  • Equation II is not an autonomous differential equation. If we isolate the derivative term, we get [MATH: x(dy)/(dx) − y^{3}|= 2; (dy)/(dx)|= (y^{3} + 2)/(x); (dy)/(dx)|= f(x, y)] where [MATH: f(x,y)= \dfrac{y^3+2}{x}.] So, it is not possible to write the equation in the form [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}=f(y).]

  • Equation III is an autonomous differential equation. Writing the equation in the form [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}=f(y),] we get [MATH: (dy)/(dx) − 3sqrt(y)|= 1; (dy)/(dx)|= 1 + 3sqrt(y); (dy)/(dx)|= f(y)] where [MATH: f(y)= 1+3\sqrt{y}.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

A first-order initial value problem (or IVP) is a first-order ordinary differential equation together with an initial condition that specifies a value of the unknown function at a point in its domain. A first-order initial value problem typically takes the form

Content:
[MATH: y' = f(x,y), \qquad y(x_0) = y_0,]

Content:
where [MATH: x_0] and [MATH: y_0] are constants.

Content:
For example,

Content:
[MATH: {\color{blue}x(2x^2-y') = -1}, \qquad {\color{red}y(e)=-2}]

Content:
is a first-order initial value problem. It consists of a first-order differential equation

Content:

Content:

sections.normalized_html:
A first-order initial value problem (or IVP) is a first-order ordinary differential equation together with an initial condition that specifies a value of the unknown function at a point in its domain. A first-order initial value problem typically takes the form

[MATH: y' = f(x,y), \quad y(x_0) = y_0,] where [MATH: x_0] and [MATH: y_0] are constants.

With that in mind, let's check each option.

  • System I is a first-order initial value problem. It consists of a first-order differential equation [MATH: x^2-3y' = y^3] together with the initial condition [MATH: y(1)=6.]

  • System II is also a first-order initial value problem. It consists of a first-order differential equation [MATH: x^3y'-e^x= \sqrt{y}] together with the initial condition [MATH: y(2)=e.]

  • System III is not a first-order initial value problem. It consists of a second-order differential equation [MATH: 2y'' - \dfrac{x}{2} = 3y'] together with two initial conditions [MATH: y(2)=3,\, y'(2) = 2.] This is a second-order initial value problem.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."
